elements.text: ASIO provides very specific limited ordering invariants in the use of a strand. The issue in this case was that two jobs are posted to the same strand object with the expectation that they are executed in the same order in which they are posted. ASIO provides this invariant in only in the case where the jobs are both posted or dispatched from the same strand, even when those operations originate from different, asynchronously chained handlers executing on that strand. In the failing test case this condition held, but the two jobs were posted from different handlers executing on the same strand. Given that the handlers were asynchronously chained, the call order was assured, and the conditions were therefore satisfied. However on Linux the invariant did not hold, and appears to require that the jobs be posted from the same handler on the strand (which means in the same thread).

attachments.text: The rise of AI agents is transforming how software can be built. The promise of agents is that developers might write code quicker, delegate multiple tasks to different agents, and even write a full piece of software purely out of natural language. In reality, what roles agents play in professional software development remains in question. This paper investigates how experienced developers use agents in building software, including their motivations, strategies, task suitability, and sentiments. Through field observations (N=13) and qualitative surveys (N=99), we find that while experienced developers value agents as a productivity boost, they retain their agency in software design and implementation out of insistence on fundamental software quality attributes, employing strategies for controlling agent behavior leveraging their expertise. In addition, experienced developers feel overall positive about incorporating agents into software development given their confidence in complementing the agents' limitations. Our results shed light on the value of software development best practices in effective use of agents, suggest the kinds of tasks for which agents may be suitable, and point towards future opportunities for better agentic interfaces and agentic use guidelines.

The fee `estimator` class is integrated into a new `node::chaser_estimate`, initialized when the node becomes current, and maintained from that point forward until shutdown. It's maintains its stack-based accumulation over a moving window of 1008 blocks (max/default) even if the node falls out of currency, and traverses reorgs.

Calls are asynchronous and passed from a protocol (e.g. electrum fee estimation method) to the base `node::protocol`, to the base `node::channel`, to the base `node::session` to the `node::full_node` to the `node::chaser_estimate` and finally to its contained estimator. This is a standard flow in the network/node architecture. The completion hander passed from the electrum method is invoked on the chaser strand, and then the electrum handler bounces it back to the electrum protocol strand for send of the tcp response.

The estimator is modeled after bitcoind fee accumulation, as this is what Electrum expects. It uses only block fee state as a very good approximation of current fee rates in comparison to analysis over unconfirmed txs. The estimator is fully unit tested, and the electrum endpoint is fully tested with empty fee data. Building a fee history for more robust testing is now over to <@U076JU78W91> for acceptance testing.

In an effort to keep the former under 1.0 hrs, I'm looking into the inbound analog to the optimization I made a few months ago, which skips object model construction when emitting full blocks or txs in wire or base16 serialization. This sped up block query a lot, but the inbound analog may significantly improve sync.

Specifically, by not parsing a block into the full object model, we can save up to 95% the memory consumption per block, since by default blocks allocate 20x their wire size using the linear accumulator. This is a big performance boost over default allocation, however at a large memory impact. Also the deserialization itself has a modest CPU hit.

Presently we obtain the txid and wtxid for each tx directly from the wire buffer. These are attached as cache within each tx object, which significantly optimizes several downstream operations, including witness and non-witness merkle root derivation. In block download we presently perform block::identity checks when under checkpoint/milestone, and full block::check() when validating. However identity is sufficient, and requires not much more from the parse than the tx hashes (also requires the coinbase witness commitment and reservation). By moving block::check to the validation phase (when full block parse is already performed for validation) we retain the simplicity of block check methods, and only have to perform block::identity using parsed hashes and coinbase data. So tonight I'm running a maxi full validation with block::check moved to the validator (full parsing on download still). This will likely not be much of a difference in time.

methods, where the message object contains the block object). In this design the identity check can be implemented by the message or passed through to the block if its been parsed (and we can implement on-demand deferred parse). The message would carry the moved socket buffer, which is then used to directly populate the store, with zero intermediate allocations. That will require a new query to write the block directly from the wire buffer into the tables. This can be done very efficiently using our rewindable fast stream parser, which is also how we obtain hashes from the buffer presently.

So there are a few steps to this. (1) parse the coinbase of witness txs to obtain the reservation and commitment hashes, and (2) move the socket buffer to the block message with a null contained block object, along with parsed tx hashes, (3) expose block identity methods on the block message for node verification, (4) implement direct buffer/hash deserialization to store serialization. But the biggest hurdle I faced in the past was dealing with block::check without a parsed block. The realization that this could move to the validator without a material performance hit makes this a lot easier.

Ok, so I promised some updated stats following the wire deserialize optimization. This was not a huge amount of work, and not terribly complex, but a lot of details to get right and tested. In all it took a calendar week.

The optimization consists of a block_view that contains a tx_view for each tx, contained within the network block message type, in place of the chain::block. The block view contains the socket buffer, which is the wire block. The view provides quick access to data within the buffer required for hashes and identity validation (merkle root and witness commitment), as well as access for store serialization. The block message still provides access to the chain::block by on-demand deserialization from the buffer, though that's not currently used.

This eliminates the population of a chain::block object for the purpose of reading from the wire and writing to the store. The chain objects are really for validation, and we only validate what is read from the store, not from the wire. From the wire we just need identity, which is much simpler and provided by the views. This is a big optimization in that it prevents the computation and memory allocation for construction and destruction of the block, which can have many tens of thousands of sub-objects. We previously optimized that using the linear memory allocator, reducing the construction down to one allocation. But this significantly over allocates the block on average, and the block itself averages 5-10x the memory of the buffer it is constructed from (in one case 20x).

In other news, after a conversation with <@U07UW5N6RQB> last night I was convinced that stripping witnesses below the milestone/checkpoint would be a fair pruning option (i.e. for nodes that want to transfer a validated full node state to a machine that is not expected to serve blocks). I ran a test of this last night, and the difference in store size was `607GiB` vs. `847GiB` at block `950k` and the milestone time dropped from `1hr to 45 mins`. This doesn't require any additional config, as it can just rely on the `peer.services_maximum` flags. By setting bit 10 (pruned) peers are notified that this node doesn't serve below depth 288. If this is set the node will now not download witness blocks below a checkpoint or active milestone. [At some point I'll also update the client filters feature so that the database table enable and archival aspect is also determined by its service bit.]
